questions.question: In the case of reflection of the light from a convex mirror, when a parallel beam of light is incident on the reflecting surface, reflected light ________.

options.text: appears to converge at the principal focus
appears to diverge from the principal focus
appears to converge at the centre of curvature
appears to diverge from the centre of curvature

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**appears to diverge from the principal focus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When a parallel beam of light is incident on a convex mirror, the reflected rays appear to diverge from a single point known as the principal focus.
 
• The principal focus is a point on the principal axis from which the reflected rays seem to originate.
 
• In a convex mirror, the principal focus is virtual, meaning it cannot be reached physically as it is located behind the mirror.
 
• This property of convex mirrors makes them useful for applications such as rearview mirrors in vehicles, where they provide a wider field of view.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Convex Mirror**

 
 
• A convex mirror is a spherical mirror in which the reflective surface bulges outward.
 
 
• **Principal Focus**
 
 
• The principal focus (F) of a mirror is the point where parallel rays of light either converge or appear to diverge after reflecting from the mirror.
 
• For a convex mirror, the principal focus is virtual and lies behind the mirror.
 
• The distance between the mirror and the principal focus is known as the focal length (f).
 
 
 
• **Reflection of Light**
 
 
• Reflection is the phenomenon where light rays bounce off a surface.
 
• The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
 
• In the case of spherical mirrors, the direction of the incident and reflected rays can be predicted using ray diagrams.
 
 
 
• **Ray Diagrams**
 
 
• Ray diagrams are graphical methods to trace the path of light rays reflecting from mirrors or passing through lenses.
 
• They help in understanding the formation and nature of the image produced by mirrors and lenses.
 
• Key rays used in ray diagrams for mirrors include the parallel ray (which reflects through the focal point), the focal ray (which reflects parallel to the principal axis), and the center of curvature ray (which reflects back along its own path).

questions.question: Twinkling of stars is related to the phenomenon of ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**refraction of light**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The twinkling of stars is primarily caused by **refraction of light** as it passes through different layers of the Earth's atmosphere.
 
• As the light from a star enters the Earth's atmosphere, it gets bent multiple times due to varying air densities, resulting in a change of direction.
 
• This constant bending of light rays makes the stars appear to twinkle or flicker from our point of view on Earth.
 
• Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another with different densities, such as from space (vacuum) into the Earth's atmosphere (air).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Interference of Light**

 
 
• Interference is a phenomenon where two or more light waves superimpose to form a resultant wave of greater, lower, or the same amplitude.
 
• It is responsible for patterns such as fringes seen in experiments like the double-slit experiment.
 
 
 
• **Reflection of Light**
 
 
• Reflection occurs when light bounces off a surface back into the original medium.
 
• It is described by the law of reflection, which states that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
 
 
 
• **Dispersion of Light**
 
 
• Dispersion is the separation of light into its constituent colors due to different degrees of refraction for different wavelengths.
 
• This phenomenon is observed when light passes through a prism, creating a spectrum of colors.

questions.question: When an object is kept at a distance 20 cm in front of a concave mirror, a real image is formed at the centre of curvature of the mirror. Magnification produced by the mirror is _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**option 2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Given that the object is placed at a distance of 20 cm in front of a concave mirror and the real image is formed at the center of curvature.
 
• The center of curvature is twice the focal length (C = 2f), which implies the focal length f is 10 cm.
 
• Since the image is formed at the center of curvature, the object distance (u) is equal to the radius of curvature (R = 2f = 20 cm).
 
• The magnification (m) produced by a concave mirror is given by the formula m = -v/u, where v is the image distance and u is the object distance.
 
• Here, v = -20 cm (real image and hence negative sign) and u = -20 cm, so m = -(-20)/-20 = -1.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Concave Mirrors**

 
 
• Concave mirrors are used to focus light and they can form real and virtual images depending on the object position relative to the focal point.
 
• They are commonly used in applications like telescopes, headlights, and shaving mirrors.
 
 
 
• **Convex Mirrors**
 
 
• Convex mirrors always form virtual, erect, and diminished images regardless of the position of the object.
 
• They are used in vehicle rear-view mirrors and in security applications because they provide a wider field of view.
 
 
 
• **Mirror Formula**
 
 
• The mirror formula relates the object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) as 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.
 
• This formula is crucial in determining the image characteristics formed by spherical mirrors.

questions.question: When an object is kept in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm, a real image is formed at a distance of 20 cm in front of the mirror. Here, the object distance is _______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**option 2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The object is kept in front of a concave mirror, which means the object distance (u) is negative according to the sign conventions of mirrors.
 
• The focal length (f) of the concave mirror is given as -10 cm (negative because it is a concave mirror).
 
• The image distance (v) is given as -20 cm (negative because the image is real and formed in front of the mirror).
 
• Using the mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, we substitute the given values to find the object distance (u).
 
• 1/(-10) = 1/(-20) + 1/u
 
• -1/10 = -1/20 + 1/u
 
• 1/u = -1/10 + 1/20
 
• 1/u = -1/20 => u = -20 cm.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Concave Mirrors**

 
 
• Concave mirrors can form both real and virtual images depending on the position of the object.
 
• They are often used in telescopes, headlights of vehicles, and shaving mirrors.
 
 
 
• **Mirror Formula**
 
 
• The mirror formula relates the object distance (u), the image distance (v), and the focal length (f): 1/f = 1/v + 1/u.
 
• This formula is applicable for both concave and convex mirrors.
 
 
 
• **Image Formation by Concave Mirrors**
 
 
• When an object is placed beyond the center of curvature, a concave mirror forms a real, inverted, and smaller image between the focal point and the center of curvature.
 
• If the object is placed at the focal point, the image formed is at infinity.

questions.question: Magnification produced by a convex mirror for a given object of height 5 cm is 0.2. Here, the height of the image is _____.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1 cm**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Magnification (m) produced by a mirror is given by the ratio of the height of the image (hᵢ) to the height of the object (hₒ).
 
• Mathematically, magnification (m) = hᵢ / hₒ.
 
• Given magnification (m) = 0.2 and height of the object (hₒ) = 5 cm.
 
• Substituting the values into the magnification formula: 0.2 = hᵢ / 5 cm.
 
• Solving for hᵢ, we get hᵢ = 0.2 * 5 cm = 1 cm.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Concave Mirror**

 
 
• Produces real and inverted images when the object is placed beyond the focal point.
 
• Produces virtual and magnified images when the object is placed between the focal point and the mirror.
 
 
 
• **Plane Mirror**
 
 
• Always produces a virtual, erect, and laterally inverted image.
 
• The size of the image is equal to the size of the object.

questions.question: The relation between focal length ‘f’, object distance ‘u’ and image distance ‘v’ in the case of reflection of light by a spherical mirror is given by ________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1/f = (1/u) + (1/v)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The formula 1/f = (1/u) + (1/v) is known as the **mirror equation** or the **mirror formula**.
 
• This equation applies to both concave and convex mirrors, with the appropriate sign conventions.
 
• In the equation, **f** represents the focal length of the mirror, **u** is the object distance from the mirror, and **v** is the image distance from the mirror.
 
• The mirror equation is derived from the geometry of the mirror and the laws of reflection.
 
• This relationship helps in determining the position and nature (real or virtual) of the image formed by spherical mirrors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sign Conventions for Spherical Mirrors**

 
 
• Distances are measured from the pole of the mirror.
 
• Distances measured in the direction of the incident light are positive, and those measured against the direction of the incident light are negative.
 
• Heights measured upward and perpendicular to the principal axis are positive, while those measured downward are negative.
 
 
 
• **Concave Mirrors**
 
 
• These mirrors can produce real and inverted images or virtual and erect images depending on the position of the object.
 
• They are used in applications like shaving mirrors, reflecting telescopes, and headlights of vehicles.
 
 
 
• **Convex Mirrors**
 
 
• Convex mirrors always produce virtual, erect, and diminished images.
 
• They are commonly used as rearview mirrors in vehicles because they provide a wider field of view.

questions.question: Magnification produced by a spherical mirror is equal to ______.

__
 
• Magnification is a measure of how much larger or smaller the image is compared to the object.
 
• It is defined as the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object.
 
• For spherical mirrors, magnification can also be related to the object distance (u) and image distance (v) by the formula: magnification (m) = -v/u.
 
• A positive magnification indicates that the image is upright, whereas a negative magnification indicates that the image is inverted.
 
• Understanding magnification helps in determining the nature and size of the image formed by mirrors and lenses.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Spherical Mirrors**

 
 
• These are mirrors with surfaces that form part of a sphere.
 
• They can be concave (converging) or convex (diverging).
 
• Concave mirrors can form real or virtual images, whereas convex mirrors always form virtual images.
 
 
 
• **Image Formation**
 
 
• The nature of the image (real or virtual, upright or inverted) depends on the position of the object relative to the mirror.
 
• Understanding the mirror equation and ray diagrams helps in predicting the nature and position of the image.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Spherical Mirrors**
 
 
• Concave mirrors are used in reflecting telescopes, makeup mirrors, and headlights.

questions.question: If a person can see far objects distinctly but cannot see nearby objects clearly, then this eye defect can be corrected by using ______.

options.text: a concave lens of suitable power
a convex lens of suitable power

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**a convex lens of suitable power**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The condition where a person can see distant objects clearly but has difficulty seeing nearby objects is called **hypermetropia** or farsightedness.
 
• Hypermetropia occurs when the eyeball is too short or the lens is not curved enough, causing light to focus behind the retina.
 
• This condition can be corrected by using a **convex lens** of suitable power.
 
• A convex lens converges light rays before they enter the eye, thus allowing the light to focus directly on the retina.
 
• Using a convex lens helps in adjusting the focal length so that nearby objects can be seen clearly.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Myopia**

 
 
• Myopia, or nearsightedness, is a condition where a person can see nearby objects clearly but has difficulty seeing distant objects.
 
• It is usually corrected using concave lenses, which diverge light rays before they enter the eye.
 
 
 
• **Astigmatism**
 
 
• Astigmatism is a common vision condition caused by an irregularly shaped cornea or lens.
 
• It can cause blurred or distorted vision at all distances and is usually corrected with cylindrical lenses.
 
 
 
• **Presbyopia**
 
 
• Presbyopia is an age-related condition where the eye's lens loses its flexibility, making it difficult to focus on close objects.
 
• This condition can be corrected using bifocal or progressive lenses that have different sections for distance and near vision.

questions.question: The distance between the centre of curvature and pole of a convex mirror of 1 m focal length is ______.
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**2m**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The distance between the **centre of curvature** and the **pole** of a mirror is called the **radius of curvature (R).**
 
• The focal length (**f**) of a spherical mirror is related to its radius of curvature (**R**) by the formula: **f = R/2.**
 
• In the given question, the focal length of the convex mirror is **1m.**
 
• Using the formula **f = R/2**, we can calculate the radius of curvature as: **R = 2f = 2 × 1 = 2m.**
 
• Thus, the distance between the **centre of curvature** and the **pole** of the convex mirror is **2m.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Focal Length (f)**__

 __
 
• The **focal length** of a mirror is the distance between its **pole** and its **focus**.
 
• For spherical mirrors, the **focal length** is always half of the **radius of curvature.**
 
• Convex mirrors are widely used in applications like **rear-view mirrors in vehicles** because they provide a **wider field of view.**
 
 
 
• **Convex Mirror**__
 __
 
• A **convex mirror** is a spherical mirror with the reflecting surface bulging outward.
 
• It always forms a **virtual, erect, and diminished image** irrespective of the object's position.
 
• It is commonly used in **security mirrors** and **traffic mirrors** for its property of diverging light rays.

 m = -(v)/(u)

questions.question: A concave mirror having focal length of magnitude 20 cm forms a real image of an object placed at a distance of 60cm from the mirror. The image distance in (cm) will be:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1**__

__**Concept:**__

**Mirror Formula for Concave Mirror:**

__
 
• The mirror formula relates the object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) of a spherical mirror.
 
• For a concave mirror, the formula is given as: (1)/(f) = (1)/(v) + (1)/(u)
 
• Object Distance (u): Distance from the object to the mirror (in cm or m). For concave mirrors, it is considered negative.
 
• Image Distance (v): Distance from the image to the mirror (in cm or m). Real images formed by concave mirrors are positive.
 
• Focal Length (f): Distance from the focal point to the mirror (in cm or m). For concave mirrors, it is negative.
 
• SI unit: The standard unit of measurement for these distances is the centimeter (cm).

**Calculation:**__

Given,

Object Distance, u = -60 cm

Focal Length, f = -20 cm

Using the mirror formula,

(1)/(f) = (1)/(v) + (1)/(u)

⇒ (1)/(-20) = (1)/(v) + (1)/(-60)

⇒ (1)/(v) = (1)/(-20) - (1)/(-60)

⇒ (1)/(v) = (-3 + 1)/(60)

⇒ (1)/(v) = (-2)/(60)

⇒ (1)/(v) = (-1)/(30)

⇒ v = -30 cm

**∴ The image distance is -30 cm.**

• Stars appear to twinkle due to the **refraction of light in the Earth's atmosphere**.
 
• The light from stars passes through various layers of the Earth's atmosphere, which have different densities and temperatures, causing **continuous bending** of light.
 
• This bending or refraction of light causes the star's light to change in intensity and position, making it appear to twinkle.
 
• The phenomenon is more pronounced for stars because they are point sources of light, unlike planets which appear larger and thus do not twinkle as much.
 
• Refraction is influenced by factors such as atmospheric turbulence, temperature gradients, and varying air pressures.

• **Atmospheric Refraction**

 
 
• Atmospheric refraction occurs when light passes through the Earth's atmosphere and bends due to varying air densities.
 
• This effect is responsible for various optical phenomena such as the apparent shift in the position of stars.
 
• Refraction also causes the sun to appear slightly shifted from its actual position during sunrise and sunset.
 
 
 
• **Scintillation**
 
 
• Scintillation refers to the rapid variations in the brightness and position of a distant luminous object, like a star, caused by small-scale fluctuations in the Earth's atmosphere.

questions.question: Which law of refraction states that light bends due to a change in speed when passing from one medium to another?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Snell's law**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Snell's law** describes the relationship between the angles of incidence and refraction when light passes through the boundary between two different isotropic media.
 
• It states that the ratio of the sines of the angles of incidence and refraction is equivalent to the ratio of the phase velocities (or equivalently, the inverse ratio of the indices of refraction) in the two media.
 
• Mathematically, Snell's law is expressed as **n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2)**, where n1 and n2 are the refractive indices of the two media, and θ1 and θ2 are the angles of incidence and refraction, respectively.
 
• Snell's law is named after the Dutch mathematician Willebrord Snellius, who formulated it in 1621.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Refractive Index**

 
 
• The refractive index of a medium is a measure of how much the speed of light is reduced inside the medium compared to the speed of light in a vacuum.
 
• It is a dimensionless number that indicates how much light is bent, or refracted, when entering a material.
 
 
 
• **Critical Angle**
 
 
• The critical angle is the angle of incidence above which total internal reflection occurs when light is passing from a medium with a higher refractive index to a medium with a lower refractive index.
 
• It can be calculated using the formula: sin(θc) = n2/n1, where θc is the critical angle, and n1 and n2 are the refractive indices of the respective media.
 
 
 
• **Fermat's Principle**
 
 
• Fermat's principle states that the path taken by light between two points is the path that can be traversed in the least time.
 
• This principle can be used to derive Snell's law and explain the behavior of light in various media.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Snell's Law**
 
 
• Snell's law is crucial in the design of lenses, prisms, and other optical instruments.
 
• It is also used in various fields such as fiber optics, astronomy, and even in the study of seismic waves in geology.

• **Concave Lens**
 
 
• A concave lens is thinner at the center than at the edges.
 
• It diverges light rays that are initially parallel, making them spread out.
 
• Commonly used in corrective lenses for myopia (nearsightedness).
 
 
 
• **Sign Convention in Optics**
 
 
• Distances measured in the direction of the incident light are taken as positive.
 
• Distances measured against the direction of the incident light are taken as negative.
 
• This convention helps in the systematic analysis of image formation by lenses and mirrors.
 
 
 
• **Focal Length**
 
 
• The focal length of a lens is the distance between the center of the lens and its focal point.
 
• It is a critical parameter in determining the imaging properties of the lens.
 
• In convex lenses, the focal length is positive, and in concave lenses, it is negative as per the sign convention.

questions.question: If the position of an object is in between the principal focus and pole of a concave mirror, then the image formed will be:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**virtual, erect and enlarged**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When an object is placed between the principal focus (F) and the pole (P) of a concave mirror, the image formed is virtual.
 
• The image is erect, meaning it is upright relative to the object.
 
• The image is also enlarged, making it appear bigger than the actual object.
 
• This phenomenon occurs because the light rays diverge after reflection and appear to come from a point behind the mirror.
 
• This property is utilized in applications like shaving mirrors and makeup mirrors where a magnified upright image is desired.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Concave Mirror:**

 
 
• A concave mirror is a spherical mirror that curves inward, resembling a portion of the interior of a sphere.
 
• It converges light rays that are incident parallel to its principal axis after reflecting them.
 
• It has applications in devices such as telescopes, head mirrors in medical examinations, and in vehicle headlights to focus light.
 
 
 
• **Principal Focus:**
 
 
• The principal focus of a concave mirror is the point where light rays parallel to the principal axis converge after reflection.
 
• It is located on the principal axis, midway between the mirror's surface and the center of curvature.
 
 
 
• **Image Formation by Mirrors:**
 
 
• The nature of the image (real or virtual, erect or inverted, magnified or diminished) depends on the position of the object relative to the mirror.
 
• Concave mirrors can form real and inverted images or virtual and erect images based on the object's placement.
 
 
 
• **Mirror Equation:**
 
 
• The relationship between the object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) of a spherical mirror is given by the mirror equation: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.
 
• This equation helps in determining the position and nature of the image formed by the mirror.
